Date:           Thursday, October 8, 2026 7:42:16 AM
Attachments:    Holtec License Amendment Comments.pdf




NRC Project Manager Marlayne Doell,

Please accept the attached public comments concerning the NRC staff's preliminary No
Significant Hazards Consideration (NSHC) determination for the proposed one-time license
amendment authorizing recovery of damaged fuel assembly DD41 at the Palisades Nuclear
Plant.

This submission is in response to the NRC's request for public comments posted on the MLive
Public Notifications page on October 7, 2026, with comments due by 4:15 p.m. Eastern Time
(ET) on October 8, 2026.

My comments address Holtec's September 30, 2026, license amendment request (PNP 2026-
052, ADAMS Accession No. ML26273A469) and raise three principal concerns:

   1. The adequacy of the NRC's preliminary NSHC determination, particularly whether
      unresolved questions concerning the original DD41 fuel-handling event have been
      adequately considered in evaluating the equipment, procedures, personnel, and
      administrative controls proposed for this unprecedented recovery.

   2. The justification for exigent processing, including whether the asserted urgency is
      supported by actual restart prerequisites and whether abbreviated public participation is
      appropriate under the circumstances.

   3. The radiological consequence evaluation, including Control Room dose assumptions,
      potential exposure to recovery personnel, and the distinction between acceptable
      accident consequences and adequate accident prevention.

My overriding concern is that demonstrating compliance with bounding radiological accident-
dose criteria is not equivalent to demonstrating that an accident will be adequately prevented.

Given the circumstances of the original DD41 event, I believe the NRC's final determination
must explicitly address the adequacy of the accident-prevention measures relied upon for this
first-of-a-kind recovery.

I respectfully request that these comments be included in the official record, considered before
the NRC finalizes its NSHC determination, and addressed in the staff's evaluation of the
proposed amendment.

Please acknowledge receipt of this submission.

Thank you for your consideration.

Respectfully,
 Alan Blind
Baroda, Michigan
      Public Comments on the NRC Sta 's Preliminary No Signi cant
     Hazards Consideration Determination

     Palisades Nuclear Plant — Proposed DD41 Fuel Assembly Recovery

     Holtec License Amendment Request: PNP 2026-052, September 30, 2026
     ADAMS Accession Number: ML26273A469
     Applicable Regulations: 10 CFR 50.92(c) and 10 CFR 50.91(a)(6)

     Overall Summary of Comments

     These three comments are directed to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission
     (NRC) sta 's preliminary determination that Holtec's proposed one-time
     recovery of damaged fuel assembly DD41 involves No Signi cant Hazards
     Consideration (NSHC).

     Although each comment addresses a di erent aspect of the proposed
     license amendment, they share a fundamental concern: the NRC's
     preliminary determination places substantial reliance on the acceptability
     of calculated accident consequences without adequately explaining how
     the circumstances that caused the original DD41 event have been
     considered in evaluating the safety of the proposed recovery.

     Comment 1 — Accident Prevention and the Adequacy of Recovery
     Controls

     This is the overriding safety concern. The proposed recovery is necessary
     because an abnormal event occurred during what should have been a
     routine reactor core-loading evolution. That event raises fundamental
     questions concerning fuel-handling equipment, design and modi cation
     controls, procedures, administrative controls, supervisory oversight,
     human performance, and corrective actions.

     The proposed recovery is substantially di erent from routine refueling.
     Reliance on existing refueling procedures and controls does not, by itself,
     demonstrate that those controls are adequate for an unprecedented
     recovery involving damaged fuel, specialized equipment, and nonstandard
     lifting and transfer operations.

                                                                fi
 The NRC must establish whether conditions that contributed to the original
event could also a ect the proposed recovery and whether the measures
credited to prevent another accident have been adequately veri ed.

Comment 2 — Exigent Processing and the Public Interest

Holtec's stated urgency is principally associated with avoiding delays in
returning Palisades to power operation. Yet Holtec reports that DD41 is
stable and under continuous surveillance, while its public statements
acknowledge that other restart activities remain outstanding.

The NRC should establish whether DD41 recovery actually controls the
projected restart date, whether the circumstances justify exigent
processing, and whether the abbreviated opportunity for public
participation is warranted.

Although exigent processing is governed separately by 10 CFR
50.91(a)(6), the decision to abbreviate review and public participation
is particularly consequential when the adequacy of accident-
prevention measures is central to the proposed NSHC determination.

Comment 3 — Radiological Consequences and Personnel Protection

Holtec's calculated accident doses remain within applicable regulatory
acceptance criteria. However, the calculated Control Room dose is
approximately 61 percent of its 5-rem criterion, and the submitted
radiological consequence calculation does not separately quantify
potential accident exposure to personnel directly performing the recovery.

These matters warrant speci c NRC consideration, particularly because
compliance with bounding accident-dose criteria does not establish
the reliability of the equipment, procedures, personnel, and
administrative controls intended to prevent the accident.

Central Concern

Demonstrating that the radiological consequences of a postulated
accident remain within regulatory acceptance criteria is not the same as
demonstrating that the accident will be adequately prevented.
      ff
                 fi
                                                    fi
           A bounding accident analysis cannot substitute for rigorous engineering,
          comprehensive procedures, personnel training and demonstrated
          pro ciency, independent safety review, or the thoroughness expected of
          the NRC's license amendment review process.

          The extraordinary circumstances that necessitated this rst-of-a-kind
          recovery demand heightened regulatory scrutiny, particularly of the
          controls intended to prevent another fuel-handling accident.

          I request that the NRC address all three comments before nalizing its
          NSHC determination and approving the proposed license amendment.



           Comment 1 — Adequacy of Accident-Prevention Measures and the
                No Signi cant Hazards Consideration Determination

          1.1 The Overriding Safety Concern

          The NRC's preliminary NSHC determination does not adequately confront
          the most troubling aspect of Holtec's proposed DD41 recovery: this
          extraordinary, rst-of-a-kind operation is necessary because normal fuel-
          handling activities resulted in a serious abnormal event whose underlying
          causes and potential programmatic implications have not been publicly
          resolved.

          Rather than examining how potential de ciencies in equipment design,
          administrative controls, supervisory oversight, procedures, or human
          performance may have contributed to the original DD41 event—and
          whether similar de ciencies could compromise the proposed recovery—
          the NRC's preliminary determination places substantial emphasis on
          Holtec's bounding accident analysis.

          Demonstrating that the radiological consequences of a postulated
          accident remain within regulatory acceptance criteria is not the same
          as demonstrating that the accident will be adequately prevented.

          A bounding accident analysis cannot substitute for rigorous engineering,
          comprehensive procedures, personnel training and demonstrated
fi
     fi
            fi

                pro ciency, independent safety review, or the thoroughness expected of
               the NRC's license amendment review process.

               The circumstances that necessitated this unprecedented recovery
               demand heightened regulatory scrutiny—not an abbreviated review
               justi ed primarily by acceptable accident consequences.

               The NRC must establish that the equipment, procedures, personnel, and
               administrative controls relied upon to prevent another fuel-handling
               accident are adequate, particularly while questions concerning the causes
               and potential programmatic implications of the original event remain
               unresolved.

               1.2 The Original DD41 Event and Its Safety Implications

               On August 30, 2026, during reactor core loading, fuel assembly DD41
               tilted approximately 30 degrees after being released by the refueling
               machine. The assembly sustained damage that prevents recovery using
               normal fuel-handling methods.

               Holtec now proposes a rst-of-a-kind, one-time recovery using specially
               designed equipment, multiple lifting and rigging evolutions, and an
               alternative fuel-transfer path that departs from the plant's existing
               licensing basis.

               The NRC sta 's preliminary determination places considerable emphasis
               on Holtec's conclusion that the proposed recovery is bounded by the
               existing fuel-handling accident analysis and that alternative equipment and
               administrative controls provide protection equivalent to normal fuel-
               handling methods.

               However, the DD41 recovery is not a normal fuel-handling evolution,
               and the circumstances that made this extraordinary recovery
               necessary cannot be separated from the evaluation of its safety
               signi cance.

               The original event raises fundamental questions regarding the adequacy of
               Holtec's fuel-handling equipment, procedures, administrative controls,
               human performance, and management oversight.
fi
     fi
          fi
                ff
                           fi
 These questions are directly relevant to the proposed recovery because
the NRC must determine whether de ciencies that contributed to the
original event could also compromise the recovery operation.

1.3 Existing Refueling Procedures Do Not, by Themselves, Establish
Adequate Recovery Controls

Of particular concern is any characterization of the proposed DD41
recovery as an evolution adequately governed by existing refueling
procedures and controls.

The recovery is not a routine refueling operation. It involves a damaged
and tilted fuel assembly, specially designed recovery equipment, multiple
lifting and rigging con gurations, and a fuel-transfer path that di ers from
the plant's existing licensing basis.

Existing refueling procedures and administrative controls may provide a
foundation for portions of the recovery. However, their existence does not
establish their adequacy for this unprecedented evolution.

Indeed, the original DD41 event occurred during activities conducted
under the plant's established fuel-handling program.

The NRC should not accept reliance on existing refueling procedures and
controls as evidence of equivalent protection without independently
establishing their applicability, identifying their limitations, and verifying the
additional engineering and procedural safeguards necessary for the
proposed recovery.

The following questions therefore warrant speci c consideration.

1. Cause and Corrective Action

Has the root cause of the DD41 event been established, its extent of
condition determined, and corrective actions su cient to prevent
recurrence implemented, consistent with 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix B,
Criterion XVI?

Have Holtec and the NRC determined whether the causes or contributing
factors of the original event could a ect the proposed recovery?

           Have appropriate corrective actions been incorporated into the recovery
          plan, and has their e ectiveness been veri ed to the extent necessary for
          the recovery?

          2. Equipment Design and Modi cation Control

          Has the NRC independently veri ed the adequacy of the design, testing,
          protective features, and 10 CFR 50.59 review associated with the recently
          installed Refueling Machine and upgraded Fuel Handling System?

          Which of these systems, components, design assumptions, protective
          features, or equipment interfaces will be relied upon during the DD41
          recovery?

          Have de ciencies or unresolved questions concerning the original
          equipment been evaluated for their potential e ect on the design, testing,
          and operation of the specialized recovery equipment?

          The NRC should establish whether equipment or design-control
          de ciencies associated with the original event could carry forward into the
          proposed recovery.

          3. Procedural and Administrative Controls

          Were the original procedures, acceptance criteria, indications, interlocks,
          and supervisory controls adequate to establish that DD41 was properly
          positioned, fully seated, and stable before the grapple was disengaged?

          Which of these procedural and administrative controls will be carried
          forward into the recovery operation?

          How has Holtec demonstrated that controls developed for routine fuel
          handling are appropriate for a damaged, tilted assembly requiring
          nonstandard lifting, rigging, and transfer operations?

          Have recovery-speci c procedures, hold points, independent veri cations,
          acceptance criteria, and contingency actions been developed and
          validated to address the limitations of existing procedures?

           The NRC should establish whether the proposed recovery procedures
          have been independently reviewed and whether personnel have
          demonstrated the ability to execute them under anticipated and credible
          abnormal conditions.

          4. Human Performance, Work Hours, and Management Oversight

          Have the potential contributions of operator performance, supervisory
          oversight, communications, workload, schedule pressure, and fatigue to
          the original event been evaluated?

          This question is particularly relevant in view of the NRC's August 12, 2026,
          exemption permitting less restrictive work-hour limitations for certain
          Operations personnel during core loading.

          Will personnel performing, directing, or supporting the DD41 recovery be
          subject to that exemption or similar work-hour arrangements?

          If so, what additional controls will ensure that fatigue, extended work
          hours, schedule pressure, and supervisory workload do not adversely
          a ect performance during this rst-of-a-kind operation?

          Have the personnel involved demonstrated pro ciency through recovery-
          speci c training, walkthroughs, and appropriate simulations?

          Have the responsibilities and authorities of operators, supervisors,
          engineering personnel, radiation protection personnel, and management
          been clearly established for each phase of the recovery?

          1.4 Relationship Between the Original Event and the Proposed Recovery

          These are not peripheral questions. They directly concern the reliability of
          the equipment, personnel, procedures, management systems, and
          administrative controls upon which Holtec now relies to justify the
          proposed recovery.

          The occurrence of the original DD41 event does not, by itself, establish
          that each of these controls failed.
ff
     fi
                             fi
                                              fi
      However, until the causes and extent of the event are understood, there
     remains an unresolved question whether the same equipment de ciencies,
     procedural weaknesses, human-performance factors, or management
     practices could adversely a ect the proposed recovery.

     The central issue is not whether Holtec has existing refueling procedures
     and administrative controls. It is whether those controls have been
     demonstrated to be adequate for this fundamentally di erent operation,
     particularly when their e ectiveness during the original fuel-handling
     evolution remains in question.

     Before nalizing its NSHC determination, the NRC should independently
     establish which existing controls are applicable, which require modi cation
     or supplementation, and what additional safeguards are necessary to
     provide reasonable assurance that the proposed recovery can be
     performed safely.

     1.5 Limitations of the Bounding Accident Analysis

     The NRC's preliminary determination states that the proposed recovery
     equipment and administrative controls provide protection equivalent to
     normal fuel-handling methods.

     Yet the abnormal event occurred during those normal fuel-handling
     activities.

     The NRC must therefore establish why the controls proposed for this
     substantially more complex evolution provide reasonable assurance of
     safety, particularly if the adequacy of the original controls remains under
     investigation.

     The bounding radiological consequence analysis is an important part of
     this evaluation, but it principally addresses the consequences of a
     postulated accident.

     It does not, by itself, establish the reliability of accident-prevention
     measures or resolve whether organizational, equipment, procedural, and
     human-performance conditions that contributed to the original event have
     been corrected.

                 Under 10 CFR 50.92(c), the NRC must determine whether the proposed
                amendment:

                1. Signi cantly increases the probability or consequences of an accident
                previously evaluated;
                2. Creates the possibility of a new or di erent kind of accident; or
                3. Signi cantly reduces a margin of safety.

                For this amendment, the accident-probability, new-or-di erent-accident,
                and margin-of-safety ndings deserve scrutiny independent of the
                calculated radiological consequences.

                The fact that a postulated accident remains within established dose
                acceptance criteria does not establish that the likelihood of an
                accident during this unusual recovery operation has been adequately
                addressed.

                The rst-of-a-kind, one-time nature of this evolution should demand
                increased rigor in engineering, independent review, procedure
                development, training, contingency planning, and management oversight
                —not reduced scrutiny because the operation will be performed only once.


                Comment 1 Conclusion

                My concern is not that a bounding accident analysis is inappropriate. It is
                that regulatory acceptability of the calculated consequences must not be
                treated as a substitute for demonstrating the adequacy of accident
                prevention.

                Until the NRC establishes that the conditions contributing to the original
                fuel-handling event have been adequately understood and addressed as
                they relate to the proposed recovery, I question whether the sta has a
                su cient basis to nalize its nding that this extraordinary operation
                involves no signi cant hazards consideration.



                Comment 2 — Public Interest and Justi cation for Exigent Processing

 2.1 Restart Schedule Urgency Versus Public Safety

Holtec's justi cation for expedited processing of the DD41 License
Amendment Request rests principally on its assertion that delaying
approval would delay activities necessary to return Palisades to power
operation.

The urgency of Holtec's restart schedule should not be confused with
an emergency involving public health and safety, nor should it
automatically justify abbreviating regulatory review and meaningful
public participation.

In Section 2.4 of its September 30, 2026, application, Holtec states that
the DD41 event was unforeseen and that delaying approval would delay
activities necessary to restore the plant to power operation.

However, Holtec's application also reports that DD41 is stable, has
exhibited no further movement, is subject to compensatory stabilization
measures, and remains under continuous camera surveillance.

The application does not identify an immediate radiological or
physical threat requiring recovery on the expedited schedule
requested by Holtec.

The proposed recovery is an extraordinary evolution involving damaged
irradiated fuel, specially designed lifting and transfer equipment, multiple
rigging operations, and movement along a path not previously authorized
by the plant's licensing basis.

Furthermore, as discussed in Comment 1, the original event raises
unresolved questions concerning equipment design, procedural adequacy,
administrative controls, supervisory oversight, and human performance.

Under these circumstances, the public interest is not adequately
addressed merely by demonstrating that expedited approval would
avoid further delay in restarting Palisades.

The public also has a substantial interest in ensuring that the causes
of the original event are understood, that the proposed recovery has
 fi
           been independently and rigorously evaluated, and that the personnel
          responsible for performing this unprecedented evolution are
          adequately prepared.

          2.2 DD41 Recovery Has Not Been Established as the Only Remaining
          Impediment to Restart

          Holtec's justi cation for expedited processing implies that prompt
          approval of the DD41 recovery amendment is necessary to avoid delaying
          an otherwise imminent return to power operation.

          That implication has not been substantiated by Holtec's public statements
          concerning the remaining work necessary for restart or by the NRC's
          established restart oversight process.

          NRC Inspection Manual Chapter 2562 establishes a comprehensive
          process for evaluating the readiness of a previously shut-down reactor to
          resume operations.

          This process includes applicable inspections, licensing activities,
          operational-readiness assessments, and review by the NRC Restart Panel
          and appropriate NRC management.

          Although Palisades has received authorization to restore its power-
          operations licensing basis, that authorization should not be confused with
          completion of all plant-speci c activities necessary to resume power
          generation.

          I am not aware of a public NRC announcement establishing that all
          remaining restart-readiness determinations, inspections, testing, and
          applicable approvals have been completed.

          More signi cantly, Holtec's September 21, 2026, public statement,
          “Progress Report on Palisades' March to Startup,” acknowledges that
          restart activities unrelated to DD41 continue.

          Holtec identi es continuing plant testing and restoration, required
          modi cations, preparations for subsequent operating modes, and
          additional commissioning activities.
fi
     fi
           fi
                fi
                           fi
 Holtec also acknowledges that progression to subsequent operating
modes remains dependent upon resolution of the a ected fuel assembly,
completion of required testing and modi cations, and applicable NRC
approvals.

These statements demonstrate that DD41 recovery is not the only
remaining prerequisite for returning Palisades to power operation.

They do not establish whether DD41 recovery is actually controlling the
projected restart date.

The NRC should therefore determine whether expedited approval would
materially advance the date of restart or whether other outstanding work
and regulatory activities independently govern that date.

If Palisades cannot yet resume power operation for reasons independent
of DD41, what public bene t is achieved by accelerating approval of this
unprecedented fuel-recovery operation at the expense of a more
deliberate regulatory review?

2.3 The Circumstances and Timing of the Request

The DD41 event occurred on August 30, 2026. Holtec submitted its
amendment request on September 30 and requested approval by October
2, allowing only two days for the requested NRC action.

Engineering and preparing a recovery plan may reasonably require
substantial time.

Nevertheless, the NRC should establish why the circumstances now
require an abbreviated regulatory process and whether the exigency could
reasonably have been avoided.

The stable condition of DD41 is particularly relevant. Holtec describes
compensatory measures and continuous surveillance intended to maintain
the assembly in its present condition.

In the absence of a demonstrated immediate safety concern requiring
prompt movement, the primary justi cation o ered for expedited
processing is the potential e ect on Holtec's restart schedule.

                                        ff
      The NRC should not permit the consequences of an abnormal event
     during routine refueling to become, by themselves, the justi cation
     for accelerating approval of an even more complex and potentially
     consequential recovery operation.

     A rst-of-a-kind fuel-recovery evolution involving damaged irradiated fuel
     warrants deliberate engineering review, independent veri cation,
     procedure validation, personnel training, contingency planning, and
     rigorous regulatory oversight.

     Its one-time nature does not diminish those obligations.

     2.4 Relationship to the NSHC Determination

     Holtec requested emergency processing under 10 CFR 50.91(a)(5), while
     the NRC's public notice describes exigent processing under 10 CFR
     50.91(a)(6).

     These are distinct regulatory procedures, and the NRC should explain the
     basis for applying the exigent process.

     I recognize that the public interest is not a separate, express legal test
     under 10 CFR 50.91(a)(6), and that restart-schedule impacts can be
     relevant to the regulatory criteria for expedited processing.

     Nevertheless, the NRC should establish the factual basis for the asserted
     urgency rather than treating a desired restart date as su cient justi cation
     in itself.

     The relationship to the preliminary NSHC nding is important.

     When a proposed amendment involves an unprecedented recovery
     necessitated by an abnormal event, shortening the opportunity for
     review and public participation increases the importance of a clear,
     independently supported determination concerning accident
     probability, accident consequences, and margins of safety.
fi
                                    fi
                                                   ffi
                                                         fi
                                                              fi
                                                                   fi
      The NRC should not allow the decision to employ exigent processing
     to diminish the rigor of its technical evaluation.


     Comment 2 Conclusion

     The central public-interest question is whether accelerating approval of the
     DD41 recovery serves a demonstrated public need or primarily serves
     Holtec's desired restart schedule.

     The public interest is served not simply by returning Palisades to
     operation as quickly as possible, but by ensuring that this
     unprecedented recovery is performed only after the necessary
     engineering, operational, personnel, and regulatory safeguards have
     been adequately established and independently evaluated.

     I request that the NRC address these considerations before nalizing its
     decision to employ exigent processing and before approving the proposed
     amendment.

     Comment 3 — Radiological Consequences and Personnel Protection
        in the No Signi cant Hazards Consideration Determination

     3.1 The Limitations of the Radiological Consequence Evaluation

     The NRC sta 's preliminary NSHC determination relies substantially on
     Holtec's radiological consequence analysis to conclude that the proposed
     DD41 recovery does not signi cantly increase the consequences of a
     previously evaluated fuel-handling accident.

     Although the calculated doses remain within applicable regulatory
     acceptance criteria, compliance with those criteria should not be
     confused with a demonstration that the proposed recovery presents
     no signi cant safety concerns, particularly for personnel directly
     involved in this extraordinary operation.
fi
      ff
           fi
                       fi
                                                      fi
 As discussed in Comment 1, the overriding concern is the adequacy of
accident prevention, given the circumstances of the original DD41 event
and the unresolved questions concerning equipment, procedures,
administrative controls, supervisory oversight, and human performance.

The radiological consequence analysis raises additional questions that
warrant speci c NRC consideration before nalizing the NSHC
determination.

3.2 Control Room Radiological Consequences

Holtec's calculation HI-2261348, Revision 1, “Radiological Consequences
of DD41 FHA at Palisades,” evaluates the consequences of a postulated
fuel-handling accident during the DD41 recovery.

The calculated radiological doses for the postulated fuel-handling accident
are as follows:
Control Room:
  • Calculated dose: 3.0402 rem TEDE
  • Acceptance criterion: 5 rem
  • Percentage of criterion: 60.8%
Exclusion Area Boundary (EAB):
  • Calculated dose: 0.56437 rem TEDE
  • Acceptance criterion: 6.3 rem
  • Percentage of criterion: 9.0%
Low Population Zone (LPZ):
  • Calculated dose: 0.069735 rem TEDE
  • Acceptance criterion: 6.3 rem
  • Percentage of criterion: 1.1%

The Control Room is the limiting analyzed receptor relative to its applicable
acceptance criterion.

Its calculated dose consists of 2.7462 rem from the postulated fuel
damage and an additional 0.294 rem from radiation shine.

A calculated Control Room dose of approximately 3.04 rem Total E ective
Dose Equivalent (TEDE) is not inconsequential simply because it remains
below the 5-rem regulatory acceptance criterion.
  fi
                                fi
                                                        ff
           It represents approximately 61 percent of the applicable dose criterion for
          this accident analysis.

          Given this utilization of the acceptance criterion, the NRC should
          independently verify the assumptions and protective measures credited to
          maintain Control Room dose within acceptable limits during the proposed
          recovery.

          This is especially important because the DD41 transfer involves movement
          of damaged irradiated fuel along an alternative path, including
          transportation outside the normal underwater fuel-transfer route.

          3.3 Control Room Ventilation and Atmospheric Dispersion
          Assumptions

          The radiological consequence calculation uses signi cantly di erent
          atmospheric dispersion factors (χ/Q) for the Control Room normal and
          emergency ventilation intakes.

          The initial atmospheric dispersion factor for the normal intake is 6.1 × 10⁻³
          sec/m³, compared with 8.32 × 10⁻⁴ sec/m³ for the emergency intake.

          Thus, for the same modeled release, the initial atmospheric concentration
          represented by the normal-intake dispersion factor is approximately 7.3
          times greater than that represented by the emergency-intake factor.

          This di erence does not translate directly into a corresponding reduction
          in calculated dose, because ventilation ow, ltration, timing, and other
          assumptions also a ect the result.

          Nevertheless, it demonstrates the importance of the ventilation
          con guration and credited protective features.

          The NRC should speci cally establish:

          1. What release locations and atmospheric dispersion assumptions are
          credited during DD41 recovery and transfer.

          2. What Control Room ventilation con gurations, isolation actions, ltration
          systems, and response times are assumed.
fi
     ff

                                     fi

                                               fi
                                                    fi
                                                              ff
                                                                   fi
      3. Whether the necessary ventilation equipment and protective features
     will be available and appropriately aligned throughout the proposed
     evolution.

     4. Whether assumptions concerning un ltered in-leakage and operator
     actions accurately represent the actual plant con guration.

     The NRC's preliminary NSHC determination does not explain how these
     assumptions were independently veri ed or what operational controls will
     ensure that the credited conditions are maintained during the recovery.

     Given that the calculated Control Room dose represents approximately 61
     percent of its acceptance criterion, these matters warrant explicit
     consideration.

     3.4 Potential Accident Dose to Personnel Performing the Recovery

     A particularly important limitation of HI-2261348 is the absence of a
     quanti ed accident-dose evaluation for personnel directly performing
     or supporting the DD41 recovery and Fuel Transfer Canister
     movement.

     The calculation evaluates the Control Room, EAB, and LPZ.

     However, personnel closest to the fuel assembly during the proposed
     evolution are not separately evaluated as accident-dose receptors in that
     calculation.

     These personnel may be involved in:

     - Retrieval of DD41 from its tilted position in the reactor vessel.
     - Attachment and operation of the specially designed Fuel Movement
     Device.
     - Lifting and placement of DD41 into the Fuel Transfer Canister.
     - Removal and movement of the loaded canister outside the normal
     underwater transfer path.
     - Transfer through the containment equipment hatch.
     - Re-rigging, upending, and subsequent placement of the canister into the
     spent-fuel-pool area.
fi
                              fi
                                   fi
                                           fi
 Holtec's LAR describes radiation protection measures, shielding
evaluations, Radiation Work Permits, activity-speci c As Low As
Reasonably Achievable (ALARA) planning, and administrative controls.

These provisions are important and should be acknowledged.

However, the presence of occupational radiation protection planning does
not, by itself, establish the potential accident dose to personnel who could
be closest to the source during the postulated fuel-handling accident.

The NRC should determine whether a separate evaluation of these
accident consequences has been performed and, if so, whether it
adequately addresses direct radiation, airborne radioactivity, shielding
degradation, personnel locations, evacuation times, and protective
actions.

If such an evaluation has not been performed, the NRC should explain
how the potential radiological consequences to these personnel have
been adequately considered in authorizing the proposed recovery.

I recognize that the accident-dose acceptance criteria under 10 CFR 50.67
and Regulatory Guide 1.183 do not necessarily require the same receptor
calculations for individual workers performing the evolution.

Nevertheless, the absence of a worker accident-dose calculation from
HI-2261348 should not be interpreted as establishing that the potential
exposure to these personnel is insigni cant.

This is an important safety consideration that warrants review
independently of the formal o site and Control Room accident-dose
acceptance criteria.

## 3.5 Bounding Accident Consequences Versus Accident Prevention

Holtec's calculation acknowledges an important uncertainty concerning
the condition of DD41.
                  ff

           Section 3.4.2 explains that the uncertain condition of the assembly
          prevents a feasible determination of how many fuel rods might be

          Consequently, Holtec conservatively assumes that all fuel rods are

          The radiological release calculation applies prescribed assumptions
          concerning the releasable radionuclide inventory; it does not assume that
          the entire radioactive inventory of the fuel is dispersed into the

          This bounding approach is a legitimate method of evaluating accident
          consequences.

          However, it does not resolve the uncertainty concerning the actual
          mechanical response of DD41 during a handling accident, nor does it
          establish the adequacy of the measures intended to prevent such an
          accident.

          The distinction is especially important because the proposed recovery
          involves damaged fuel, specially fabricated handling equipment, multiple

          The NRC's preliminary determination states that the proposed recovery

          The radiological consequence calculation supports an assessment of the
          consequences of a postulated accident.

          It does not, standing alone, demonstrate the adequacy of the lifting
          equipment, rigging arrangements, procedural controls, personnel
          pro ciency, or contingency measures necessary to prevent the accident.

          The acceptability of a postulated accident's consequences must not
          become a substitute for demonstrating that the accident has been
          adequately prevented.

     Comment 3 Conclusion

     The NRC's preliminary determination emphasizes that the calculated
     radiological consequences of a postulated DD41 fuel-handling accident
     remain within regulatory acceptance criteria.

     That conclusion does not resolve the fundamental safety questions
     associated with this unprecedented recovery operation.

     The Control Room calculation uses approximately 61 percent of its
     applicable acceptance criterion. The submitted radiological consequence
     calculation does not separately quantify potential accident dose to
     personnel directly performing the recovery.

     Moreover, the bounding accident calculation cannot, by itself, establish
     that the proposed equipment, procedures, administrative controls, and
     personnel preparations adequately prevent the accident.

     These concerns reinforce the overriding issue presented in Comment 1:
     the NRC must establish reasonable assurance that conditions associated
     with the original fuel-handling event will not compromise the safety of the
     proposed recovery.

     For a rst-of-a-kind, infrequently performed evolution involving damaged
     irradiated fuel, the proper regulatory emphasis must be on rigorous
     accident prevention as well as acceptable accident consequences.

     I request that the NRC explicitly address these matters before nalizing its
     NSHC determination and approving the proposed DD41 license
     amendment.

              Overall Conclusion and Requested NRC Determination

     Taken together, these three comments question whether the NRC sta has
     established an adequate basis for its preliminary nding of No Signi cant
     Hazards Consideration.

     Comment 1 remains the overriding concern: an abnormal event occurred
     during routine fuel handling, and the proposed recovery now relies upon
     equipment, personnel, procedures, and administrative controls whose
     applicability and adequacy for this substantially di erent operation must
     be independently established.

     Comment 2 raises the additional concern that an accelerated restart
     schedule should not substitute for a demonstrated basis for exigent
     processing, particularly when other restart activities remain outstanding
     and the a ected fuel assembly is reported to be stable.

     Comment 3 establishes that acceptable calculated radiological
     consequences do not, by themselves, resolve questions concerning
     Control Room protection, recovery-personnel exposure, or the adequacy
     of accident-prevention measures.

     The NRC should not interpret compliance with bounding radiological
     accident-dose criteria as resolving the distinct questions of accident
     probability, equipment and administrative-control reliability, the possibility
     of new or di erent accidents, or margins of safety.

     Nor should the desire to avoid restart delays displace the engineering
     rigor, personnel preparation, and regulatory oversight appropriate to a rst-
     of-a-kind recovery involving damaged irradiated fuel.

     The central issue is not simply whether the consequences of a postulated
     accident remain within regulatory limits. It is whether the NRC has
     independently established that the proposed recovery can be performed
     with adequate controls to prevent the accident in the rst place.
